Date: 2023-02-27
REMARKS
Claims 21, 23-27, 29, 31-37, and 39-50 are pending. Claims 1-20, 22, 28, 30, and 38 were previously cancelled. Claims 21 and 40 have been amended without prejudice to, or disclaimer of, the underlying subject matter. Support for the amendments may be found in the original claims and specification, e.g., at [0115], Table 2. No new matter enters by way of the present amendments. Reconsideration of the application based on the above amendments and following remarks is respectfully requested.
Reiections under 35 U.S.C. 103
A. Claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37
Claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2016/0338591 to Lachenbruch et al. ("Lachenbruch") in view of U.S. 2015/0186607 to Geleijnse et al. ("Geleijnse"), further in view of "Capacitive Biosensors" to Berggren et al. ("Berggren"). See Office Action at 6.
Specifically, the Examiner alleges that "Lachenbruch et al. teaches a method of providing a continuity of for a patient at risk of developing pressure ulcers (PU) during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting, the method comprising the steps of: results as results obtained from performing a first SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient while in the first care setting, ... wherein the first SEM scan comprises a plurality of measurements of an SEM value at the body location ... and calculation of a first delta value from the plurality of SEM values." Id. The Examiner concedes that Lachenbruch "does not explicitly teach a current intervention as well as the optionality to change the intervention based on the measurements."
Id. at 8. However, the Examiner cites Geleijnse for providing "identifying a current PU intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting... wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record... do nothing by continuing to administer the current PU intervention. . . do something by administering a new PU intervention of level-N, where N has a value greater than K." Id. at 8-9. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) identify a current PU intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting, wherein the current PU intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record, 2) continue to administer the current PU intervention, and 3) administer a new PU intervention of level-N, where N has a value greater than K as taught by Geleijnse et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al. with the motivation(s) of monitoring a patient's condition and adjusting the level of care accordingly." Office Action at 9. Furthermore, the Examiner cites Berggren for providing "calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements," and concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute 4) calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements as taught by Berggren for the collection of other values as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al. and Geleijnse et al. in combination (more particularly, paragraph [0037] of Lachenbruch et al.) since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements."
Id. at 9-10.
In response to Applicant's previous arguments filed on August 22, 2022, that there are unexpected results in the presently claimed method, the Examiner apparently disagrees for three reasons. See id. at 3. The Examiner alleges that "[f]irst, the claims are broader in scope than the scenario that is being argued with respect to the unexpected results. Second, the evidence provided cannot be evidence as the Musa reference is not completely commensurate with the claimed invention. Third, the results of improvement in care based on patient data is not unexpected." Id. Regarding the first and second reasons, the Examiner alleges that the previously cited Musa reference ("Musa") "is not related to the claimed invention even if it offers similar subject matter[,]" and that "[t]he evidence is not attributable to the claimed invention but rather attributable to an outside source." Id. at 4. Regarding the third reason, the Examiner "questions how changing care based on patient measurements can be considered unexpected[,]" and cites to Geleijnse alleging that it teaches "that a patient's condition is monitored and care is adjusted to be better tailored to a patient in paragraphs [0002] and [0004]."
Id. The Examiner acknowledges that "Applicant is trying to highlight that the present invention improves these numbers when there is a transition of care across two settings where the settings may provide that variability of uncertainty[,]" however, the Examiner further alleges that "one can argue that the goals for both the claimed invention and the Geleijnse reference (where the goal is improvements in treatment results based on monitoring a patient's status) are the same meaning that the results should be expected." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
At the outset, without acquiescing to the rejection, and solely to advance prosecution, claim 21 has been amended to recite "wherein if the current PU intervention of level-K is a level-0 PU intervention, the level-0 PU intervention comprises performing a daily SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient." Applicant has amended claim 21 to recite features of claim 40.
Applicant respectfully disagrees that aprimafacie case of obviousness has been established for claim 21 for at least the following three reasons: (a) Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, alone or in combination, do not provide or suggest each and every element of amended claim 21; (b) a person of ordinary skill in the art combining the cited references would not have arrived at the claimed subject matter with a reasonable expectation of success; and (c) the claimed method yields unexpected results.
(a) Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, alone or in combination, do not provide or suggest each and every element of amended claim 21 Applicant respectfully submits that Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, alone or in combination, do not provide or suggest each and every element of amended claim 21.
It is well-established law for an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 that the references, either alone or combined, must provide all of the elements of the claim. The Office is required to make "a searching comparison of the claimed invention - including all its limitations - with the teaching of the prior art." In re Ochiai, 71 F.3d 1565, 1572 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and CFMT v. Yieldup Intern. Corp., 349 F.3d 1333, 1342 (Fed. Cir. 2003). When "[t]he prior art reference (or references when combined) [do] not teach or suggest all the claim limitations, ... [o]ffice personnel must explain why the difference(s) between the prior art and the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art." M.P.E.P. at § 2141 (III).
The Examiner has not at least shown that the cited references, alone or in combination, provide or suggest that wherein if the current PU intervention of level-K is a level-0 PU intervention, the level-0 PU intervention comprises performing a daily SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient.
The Examiner acknowledges that Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren "in combination may not specifically, further teach ... a level-0 PU intervention ... ." Office Action at p. 23. Indeed, Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren, alone or in combination, are silent regarding a level-0 PU intervention, much less that the level-0 PU intervention comprises performing a daily SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient. The Examiner goes on to cite Brem et al. "Protocol for the successful treatment of pressure ulcers" ("Brem"), to provide "wherein a level-0 PU intervention is selected from the group consisting of providing good nutrition, standard mattress, turning every 24 hours, and a combination thereof" Id. at p. 24. Applicant respectfully submits that Brem, at best, provides a protocol for treating pressure ulcers in the context of "[d]aily visual assessment of the skin," and involves "[o]bjective measurement of every wound by photography ... and thorough documentation of wound's progress with a graph." Brem at 12S, points 2 and 3 under Protocol for the comprehensive treatment of pressure ulcers. A person of ordinary skill in the art reading Brem as a whole would understand that Brem's disclosure is focused on preventing stage IV ulcers, which is the most advanced stage of ulcers, using visual assessment. See id. at 9S. This is different than Applicant's disclosure which addresses "a clear need to identify tissue damage earlier so that interventions can prevent progression of the subepidermal damage to stage-1 and beyond." Specification at [0154]. Applicant's disclosure clearly indicates that the disclosed methods are useful for preventing pressure ulcers prior to stage-1 as shown in Figure 6D "[i]n some instances, the tissue may be considered to be 'stage 1' pressure ulcer after time t4." Id. at [0135] and [0138]. Additionally, Applicant's specification provides that level-0 PU intervention comprises a frequency of subsequent SEM measurement at every 24 hours (daily). See Specification at Table 2. In contrast, Brem is silent regarding using SEM measurements for assessing early stage ulcers, much less that a level-0 PU intervention comprises performing a daily SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient.
For at least the above reasons, Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, alone or in combination, do not provide or suggest each and every element of amended claim 21.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the amended claim 21 is nonobvious over Lachenbruch, in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem.
(b) A person of ordinary skill in the art combining the cited references would not have arrived at the claimed subject matter with a reasonable expectation of success
Notwithstanding that Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, alone or in combination, do not provide or suggest all the elements of amended claim 21, the Examiner "questions how changing care based on patient measurements can be considered unexpected[,]" and further alleges that "one can argue that the goals for both the claimed invention and the Geleijnse reference ... are the same meaning that the results should be expected." Office Action at 4. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
To establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, there must be some suggestion or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings. There must also be a reasonable expectation of success. The teaching or suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art, and not based on the applicant's disclosure. In re Vaeck, 947 F.2d 488, 20 USPQ2d 1438 (Fed. Cir. 1991) (emphasis added).
One of ordinary skill in the art combining Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem would not have arrived at the claimed subject matter of amended claim 21 with a reasonable expectation of success. When read as a whole, Brem at best provides visual assessment to prevent advanced stage of ulcer formation (stage IV). Brem at 9S and 12S. As previously discussed in Section A(a), Brem provides an ulcer assessment method based on visual inspection that is different from Applicant's claimed method based on SEM measurements. Accordingly, one of ordinary skill in the art would understand that there would not be a reasonable expectation of success to apply a known element of Brem's assessment protocol to Applicant's assessment protocol to achieve an alleged comparable result. For example, there is no reasonable expectation of success found in the prior art, or generally in the art, in applying the frequency of daily (every 24 hours) visual assessments disclosed in Brem to Applicant's SEM measurements for effectively preventing early stage ulcers. In view of this lack of reasonable expectation of success, a person of ordinary skill in the art would not have combined Brem with Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, and Berggren as alleged by the Examiner.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that amended claim 21 is nonobvious over Lachenbruch, in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem.
(c) The claimed method yields unexpected results
Furthermore, even if assuming arguendo that there is motivation to combine Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem to arrive at the instant claims (Applicant does not concede), Applicant maintains that the claimed subject matter yields unexpected results. The Examiner alleges that "Musa is not related to the claimed invention even if it offers similar subject matter[,]" and that "[t]he evidence is not attributable to the claimed invention but rather attributable to an outside source." Office Action at 4. Applicant respectfully submits that Musa unambiguously uses "a medical device, the sub-epidermal moisture (SEM) scanner (Bruin Biometrics, LLC, US) to identify the presence of SEM in the tissue[,]" and that "[t]raining was supported by Bruin Biometrics LLC ... all nursing staff were fully trained in the correct procedure for using the SEM Scanner, the relevance of recognizing a raised delta and the need to adjust clinical interventions accordingly." Musa at 4 and 6. In view of the amendments to claim 21, together with the reasons provided above, Applicant respectfully submits that the instant claims are commensurate with the evidence as provided in Musa.
Finally, even assuming arguendo that it would be expected to achieve some degree of improvement in patient care using the claimed method (Applicant does not concede), the claimed method provides an unexpectedly high level of patient benefits, which establishes the non-obviousness of the claimed method. Specifically, as described in Musa, the claimed method for continuity of care reduced incidence of PU by 87.2% in acute care settings, and as much as 100% at 10 of the 15 test sites. Musa at 2. In other words, the incidence of PUs was surprisingly completely eliminated in a majority of test sites. The Examiner has not provided any objective evidence that a person of ordinary skill in the art combining the cited references to arrive at the claim method, would have had the expectation that the claimed method would achieve a 100% incidence reduction of PU in a majority of test sites. The unexpected degree of improvement in patient care resulting from the claimed method is sufficient to overcome any prima facie case of obviousness the Examiner could have raised.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 21, 23-26, 29, and 37 under 35 U.S.C. §103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem.
B. Claim 27
Claim 27 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,028,407 to Bennet-Guerrero ("Bennet-Guerrero"). See Office Action at 15.
Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Bennet-Guerrero provides "continuing to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold." Id. at 15. As such, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time [] the invention was filed would have found it obvious to continue to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold as taught by Bennett-Guerrero in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to store and retrieve information from a database." Id. at 15-16. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 27 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Bennet-Guerrero does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 27 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 27 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of Bennet-Guerrero.
C. Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39
Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 29, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,675,289 to Heaton ("Heaton"). See Office Action at 16.
Specifically for claim 31, the Examiner alleges that Heaton provides "querying the database for data to form retrieved data values (see FIG. 9 where there is a directory for storing and retrieving archived responses into and from the database. In order for the system here to access the database here, it would query the database in order to retrieve the necessary data)." Id. at 16. As such, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time the invention was filed would have found it obvious to query the database for data to form retrieved delta values as taught by Heaton in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to store and retrieve information from a database." Id at 17. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are dependent directly or indirectly from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Heaton does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 31-32, 34, and 39 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 29, and further in view of Heaton.
D. Claim 33
Claims 33 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 29, and further in view of U.S. 2008/0015894 to Miller et al. ("Miller"). See Office Action at 19-20. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Miller provides "creating an additional data record, wherein the data element comprises one or more of a nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, an event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result," and "reporting the additional data record to the database." Id. at 20.
Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) create an additional data record, wherein the data element comprises... and 2) report the additional data record to the database as taught by Miller et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al. and Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination with the motivation(s) of updating a patient files." Id. at 20-21. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 33 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Miller does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 33 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 33 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 29, and further in view of Miller.
E. Claims 35-36
Claims 35-36 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and further in view of Heaton as applied to claim 32, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,355,925 to Rothman et al. ("Rothman"). See Office Action at 21. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Rothman provides "the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value." Id. at 21. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time [] the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to- intercept of a selected threshold value as taught by Rothman et al. in the method as taught by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., Berggren, and Heaton in combination with the motivation(s) of alerting a user if a patient is getting better or worse at an accelerating rate." Id. at 22.
Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claims 35 and 36 are dependent directly or indirectly from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Rothman does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claims 35 and 36 are also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 35 and 36 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem, further in view of Heaton as previously applied to claim 32, and further in view of Rothman.
F. Claims 40 and 43
Claims 40 and 43 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Protocol for the successful treatment of pressure ulcers" to Brem et al. ("Brem"). See Office Action at 23. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Brem provides "wherein a level-0 PU intervention is selected from the group consisting of providing good nutrition, standard mattress, turning ever 24 hours, and a combination thereof," and "a level-3 PU intervention of applying dressing to the back or sides of patient's heel." Id. at 23-24. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a group consisting of providing good nutrition, standard mattress, turning every 24 hours, and a combination thereof as taught by Brem et al. for the group as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claims 40 and 43 are dependent directly or indirectly from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, claims 40 and 43 are also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 40 and 43 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21.
G. Claim 41
Claim 41 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 5,367,789 to Lamont ("Lamont"). See Office Action at 25. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Lamont provides a level-1 PU intervention of providing a heel boot to the patient. Id. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-1 PU intervention of providing a heel boot to the patient as taught by Lamont for a treatment level as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 41 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Lamont does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 41 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 41 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of Lamont.
H. Claim 42
Claim 42 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,634,045 to DuDonis et a. ("DuDonis"). See Office Action at 26. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that DuDonis provides "a level-2 PU intervention of changing the patient's support surface." I. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-2 PU intervention of changing the patient's support surface as taught by DuDonis for a treatment level as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 42 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and DuDonis does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 42 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 42 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of DuDonis.
I. Claim 44
Claim 44 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Friction between human skin and medical textiles for decubitus prevention" to Rotaru et al.
("Rotaru"). See Office Action at 28. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Rotaru provides a level-4 PU intervention of changing the patient's sheet cover to a low-friction sheet cover. Id.
Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-4 PU intervention of changing the patient's sheet cover to a low-friction sheet cover as taught by Rotaru, for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. at 27-28. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 44 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Rotaru does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 44 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 44 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of Rotaru.
J. Claim 45
Claim 45 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,011,041 to Hann ("Hann"). See Office Action at 29-30. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Hann provides "a level-5 PU intervention of providing a low-friction padded mattress surface for the patient's lower leg." Id Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-5 PU intervention of providing a low-friction padded mattress surface for the patient's lower leg as taught by Hann for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. at 28-29. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. I re Pine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Claim 45 is dependent from claim 21, and incorporates the features of claim 21. Since the Examiner has not shown that claim 21 is obvious in view of Lachenbruch, Geleijnse, Berggren, and Brem, and Hann does not remedy the deficiencies of these references, claim 45 is also nonobvious.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 45 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren and Brem as previously applied to claim 21, and further in view of Hann.
K. Claims 46 and 47
Claims 46 and 47 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Lachenbruch in view of Geleijnse, further in view of Berggren as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Prevention and Treatment of Pressure Ulcers" to Thomas ("Thomas"). See Office Action at 30. Specifically, the Examiner alleges that Thomas provides "a level-6 PU intervention of turning the patient at a shorter interval than currently provided for," and "a level- 7 PU intervention of applying a barrier cream to the patient's heel." Id. at 29-30. Thus, the Examiner concludes that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute [the interventions]. . . as taught by Thomas for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Lachenbruch et al., Geleijnse et al., and Berggren in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements. Id. at 29-30. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
If an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988).
